hints.title: Concept
hints.body: A flat array and a table hold the same numbers; only the way you count positions differs. Reshaping changes the shape, never the values or their order.

hints.title: Syntax or concept to use
hints.body: `arr.reshape(rows, cols)` returns the array in the new shape, and the product of the new dimensions must equal the number of elements. `arr.shape` reports the current shape and `tolist()` gives plain nested lists.

hints.title: Approach
hints.body: Build the twelve numbers so that they run from 1 to 12 (remember that `arange` excludes its stop value), reshape them to four rows and three columns, then print the nested list and the shape.

hints.title: Structured steps
hints.body:
```python
import numpy as np

nums = np.arange(..., ...)   # 1 through 12 inclusive
table = nums.reshape(..., ...)
print(table.tolist())
print(table.shape)
```

debugging.symptom: `ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 12 into shape (4,4)`.
debugging.cause: The requested rows times columns (16) does not equal the 12 elements.
debugging.fix: Choose dimensions whose product is 12, here 4 rows and 3 columns.

debugging.symptom: The first row prints `[0, 1, 2]` instead of `[1, 2, 3]`.
debugging.cause: The array was built with `np.arange(12)`, which starts at 0 and stops at 11.
debugging.fix: Start at 1 and stop at 13, because the stop value is excluded.

debugging.symptom: The table prints `(3, 4)`, with the dimensions swapped.
debugging.cause: `reshape(3, 4)` takes rows first, so the arguments are in the opposite order to the request.
debugging.fix: Put the number of rows first and columns second.

constraints: Line 1 is a nested list, line 2 is the shape tuple.
daily:d063#g3.realWorld: Sensor and image data arrive as one long stream; reshaping it into rows and columns (days by hours, height by width) is the first step of almost every analysis.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that the stop of arange is exclusive.
Printing the array instead of `tolist()`, which uses a different format.

alternatives.title: Let NumPy infer one dimension
alternatives.code:
import numpy as np

nums = np.arange(1, 13)
table = nums.reshape(4, -1)
print(table.tolist())
print(table.shape)
alternatives.note: `-1` means 'work this dimension out'. It avoids hand-multiplying sizes when the data length changes, but it hides mistakes: if the length is not divisible you get an error only at run time, and a wrong row count silently produces a different valid table.

hints.title: Concept
hints.body: Comparing an array with a number does not give one answer, it gives an answer for every element. That array of yes/no values is a mask.

hints.title: Syntax or concept to use
hints.body: `arr[mask]` keeps the elements where the mask is True. A boolean array can be summed, because True counts as 1.

hints.title: Approach
hints.body: Build a mask for 'at least 100' and use it to select values; count the values below 100 with a second mask and a sum.

hints.title: Structured steps
hints.body:
```python
import numpy as np

sales = np.array([120, 85, 240, 60, 310, 95])
print(sales[...].tolist())   # mask: at least 100
print((...).sum())           # how many are below 100
```

debugging.symptom: `ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous`.
debugging.cause: `if sales >= 100:` or `sales >= 100 and ...` uses Python logic on a whole array.
debugging.fix: Use the mask as an index, or combine masks with `&` and `|` in parentheses.

debugging.symptom: Line 1 prints `[True, False, True, False, True, False]`.
debugging.cause: The mask itself was printed instead of using it to index the array.
debugging.fix: Put the mask inside the square brackets of the array.

debugging.symptom: Line 2 prints the list of values instead of a count.
debugging.cause: The mask was applied as an index (`sales[sales < 100]`), which returns elements, not their number.
debugging.fix: Sum the boolean mask, or count its True values.

constraints: Line 1 is a list of the values that are 100 or more, in original order.
daily:d064#g2.realWorld: Every analysis starts by selecting the rows that match a rule: orders over a limit, sensors above a threshold, scores below a pass mark.
commonMistakes: Using `>` where the rule says 'at least'.

alternatives.title: Index array from nonzero
alternatives.code:
import numpy as np

sales = np.array([120, 85, 240, 60, 310, 95])
idx = np.nonzero(sales >= 100)[0]
print(sales[idx].tolist())
print(np.count_nonzero(sales < 100))
alternatives.note: A mask has one boolean per element; an index array lists the positions. Index arrays are useful when you need the positions themselves (to update other arrays or report where) but they cost an extra array. For a plain filter the boolean mask is shorter.

hints.title: Concept
hints.body: NumPy can show you the same memory through a window or hand you a private copy. Which one you get depends on how you selected the elements.

hints.title: Syntax or concept to use
hints.body: Basic slicing (`a[:3]`) returns a view. Boolean masks and index lists (`a[a > 3]`) return a copy. `np.shares_memory(x, y)` tells you which case you are in.

hints.title: Approach
hints.body: Edit through the slice and print the original, then edit through the masked result and print the original again, then ask `shares_memory` for each. Predict each line before running.

hints.title: Structured steps
hints.body:
```python
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
v = a[...]      # slice
v[0] = 100
print(a.tolist())
c = a[...]      # mask selection
c[0] = 0
print(a.tolist())
print(np.shares_memory(a, v))
print(np.shares_memory(a, c))
```

debugging.symptom: `a` is unchanged after `v[0] = 100`.
debugging.cause: `v` was created with `.copy()` or from a mask, so it owns its own data.
debugging.fix: Take a plain slice, which is a view onto `a`.

debugging.symptom: The second print shows `0` inside `a`.
debugging.cause: A mask result was expected to be a view, but fancy indexing always copies.
debugging.fix: Remember: slice means view, mask or index list means copy.

debugging.symptom: `shares_memory` prints the same value twice.
debugging.cause: Both variables were created the same way (both slices or both masks).
debugging.fix: Create `v` by slicing and `c` by masking.

constraints: Four output lines: two lists and two booleans.
The array must be changed only by the first edit.
daily:d064#g4.realWorld: Accidentally modifying a view corrupts the original dataset; accidentally copying large arrays wastes memory. Knowing which operation does which is a daily debugging skill.
commonMistakes: Assuming every selection behaves like a Python list slice (which copies).

hints.title: Concept
hints.body: Vectorising means writing the arithmetic once and letting NumPy apply it to every element, instead of looping in Python.

hints.title: Syntax or concept to use
hints.body: Arithmetic operators (`*`, `/`, `+`) work element by element on arrays. A comparison creates a mask that can index the new array.

hints.title: Approach
hints.body: Compute the Fahrenheit array in one expression and keep it in a variable, then print it, and print the part of it selected by a mask on the same array.

hints.title: Structured steps
hints.body:
```python
import numpy as np

celsius = np.array([0, 25, 100, -40])
f = ...                  # conversion formula on the whole array
print(f.tolist())
print(f[...].tolist())   # mask: above 70
```

debugging.symptom: `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for *: 'list' and 'float'`.
debugging.cause: The formula is applied to a plain Python list instead of the array.
debugging.fix: Operate on `celsius`, which is an array.

debugging.symptom: The Fahrenheit list is printed but the masked line is empty or wrong.
debugging.cause: The mask was built from `celsius > 70` rather than from the converted values.
debugging.fix: Mask the Fahrenheit array.

debugging.symptom: Output shows integers such as `32` instead of `32.0`.
debugging.cause: Integer division (`//`) or a conversion to int removed the decimals.
debugging.fix: Use true division `/`, which returns floats.

constraints: Use array arithmetic, not a loop.
daily:d065#g1.realWorld: Unit conversion across a whole column of readings is the standard case for vectorised arithmetic, and it is much faster than a Python loop on large data.
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the list with a for loop.

alternatives.title: List comprehension then array
alternatives.code:
import numpy as np

celsius = np.array([0, 25, 100, -40])
f = np.array([c * 9 / 5 + 32 for c in celsius])
print(f.tolist())
print(f[f > 70].tolist())
alternatives.note: Gives the same values, but the arithmetic runs in the Python interpreter one element at a time. For four values it does not matter; for millions it is typically one to two orders of magnitude slower than the vectorised expression, which is why NumPy code avoids it.

hints.title: Concept
hints.body: Broadcasting stretches a smaller array across a larger one, but only along axes whose sizes match or equal 1. A row of 3 fits the columns of a 2-by-3 table; a list of 2 needs to become a column first.

hints.title: Syntax or concept to use
hints.body: Shapes are compared from the right. `(2, 3) + (3,)` works. `(2, 3) + (2,)` does not, but `(2, 3) + (2, 1)` does. `arr[:, None]` or `arr.reshape(-1, 1)` turns a 1-D array into a column.

hints.title: Approach
hints.body: Add the three-element array directly for the first line. For the second, turn the two-element array into a column of shape (2, 1) before adding it.

hints.title: Structured steps
hints.body:
```python
import numpy as np

t = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print((t + np.array([10, 20, 30])).tolist())
print((t + np.array([100, 200])...).tolist())   # make it a column
```

debugging.symptom: `ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,3) (2,)`.
debugging.cause: A 1-D array of length 2 is aligned with the last axis (length 3), which does not match.
debugging.fix: Give it shape (2, 1) so it lines up with the rows.

debugging.symptom: `ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 2 into shape (3,2)`.
debugging.cause: The two row offsets were reshaped to the shape of the table (or its transpose) instead of to a column that has one entry per row.
debugging.fix: Reshape to two rows and one column (`-1, 1` lets NumPy infer the rows) and let broadcasting stretch it.

debugging.symptom: `[:, None]` was applied to the 2-D table instead of the helper array.
debugging.cause: The new axis was added to the wrong array, which changes the table's shape.
debugging.fix: Insert the axis into the 1-D array of per-row offsets.

daily:d065#g3.realWorld: Adding a per-column baseline or a per-row offset to a table is broadcasting; it replaces loops over rows in nearly every numeric workflow.
commonMistakes: Thinking NumPy guesses which axis you meant.

alternatives.title: Explicit tile and repeat
alternatives.code:
import numpy as np

t = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print((t + np.tile(np.array([10, 20, 30]), (2, 1))).tolist())
print((t + np.repeat(np.array([100, 200]), 3).reshape(2, 3)).tolist())
alternatives.note: tile and repeat materialise the full 2-by-3 arrays before adding, which makes the shapes visible and is a good way to check your understanding. Broadcasting does the same result without allocating those copies, which matters when the table is large.

hints.title: Concept
hints.body: A table has two directions. Collapsing one direction removes it from the result: sum over the rows and you are left with one value per column.

hints.title: Syntax or concept to use
hints.body: `arr.sum(axis=0)` adds down the rows (one total per column); `axis=1` adds across the columns (one total per row). The axis you name is the one that disappears.

hints.title: Approach
hints.body: Products are columns, so the total per product collapses the day (row) axis. The total per day collapses the product axis.

hints.title: Structured steps
hints.body:
```python
import numpy as np

t = np.array([[3, 5, 7], [2, 4, 6]])
print(t.sum(axis=...).tolist())   # one total per product
print(t.sum(axis=...).tolist())   # one total per day
```

debugging.symptom: The two lines are swapped: `[15, 12]` first.
debugging.cause: `axis=1` was used for the per-product total, but it sums across columns.
debugging.fix: Use `axis=0` for column totals.

debugging.symptom: Output is a single number `27`.
debugging.cause: `t.sum()` without axis adds all elements.
debugging.fix: Name the axis to keep the other dimension.

debugging.symptom: `AxisError: axis 2 is out of bounds for array of dimension 2`.
debugging.cause: A 2-D array only has axes 0 and 1.
debugging.fix: Use 0 or 1.

constraints: Line 1 has one entry per product, line 2 one per day.
daily:d066#g2.realWorld: Totals per product and per day from the same grid are the two margins of every report table.
commonMistakes: Memorising 'axis 0 is rows' instead of 'the named axis disappears'.

hints.title: Concept
hints.body: Standardising puts every column on the same scale: subtract the column's mean and divide by its standard deviation. The statistics belong to columns, but the subtraction happens on every row.

hints.title: Syntax or concept to use
hints.body: `x.mean(axis=0)` and `x.std(axis=0)` give one value per column (population standard deviation by default). They have shape (2,), which broadcasts against the rows of a (3, 2) table.

hints.title: Approach
hints.body: Compute the column mean and standard deviation, standardise with one expression, and print the three results, rounding standard deviations and z-scores to 3 decimals.

hints.title: Structured steps
hints.body:
```python
import numpy as np

x = np.array([[100.0, 2.0], [160.0, 5.0], [220.0, 11.0]])
mean = x.mean(axis=...)
std = x.std(axis=...)
z = (x - ...) / ...
print(mean.tolist())
print(np.round(std, 3).tolist())
print(np.round(z, 3).tolist())
```

debugging.symptom: Means are `[160.0, 6.0]` expected, but the output has three values.
debugging.cause: The statistics were taken with `axis=1`, which gives one per row.
debugging.fix: Take them down the rows with `axis=0`.

debugging.symptom: `ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,2) (3,)`.
debugging.cause: Per-row statistics (shape (3,)) cannot be subtracted from a (3, 2) table.
debugging.fix: Use per-column statistics of shape (2,).

debugging.symptom: The z-scores differ from the expected ones: the first row is `[-1.0, -0.873]` instead of `[-1.225, -1.069]`.
debugging.cause: The sample standard deviation (`ddof=1`) was used while the exercise asks for the population one.
debugging.fix: Keep the default `ddof=0`.

constraints: Rounded to 3 decimals only when printing.
daily:d066#i1.realWorld: Standardised features are the input of nearly every distance-based model (clustering, k-NN) so that spend in dollars does not drown visit counts.
